## 1 Introduction

Civil wars and intrastate armed con ict broadly de ned are the predomi 
nant forms of organized violence in the contemporary era, and they occur 
throughout the world (Figure 1.1). Between 1946 and 2023, a total of 2,686 
intrastate armed con icts occurred, of which 462 were internationalized. 
Approximately half of all states experienced domestic armed con ict of 
some sort, and in many cases recurring, multiple con icts. Moreover, the 
historical trend to 2023 is upward. Intrastate armed con icts increased 
from eight in 1946 to thirty-seven in 2023, while internationalized intra 
state armed con icts increased from two to twenty during the same period 
(see Figure 1.2 and Appendix A). During that period, Africa was the most 
af icted by intrastate and internationalized intrastate armed con icts, 
with Asia next (see Appendix B). In line with these upward trends, civil 
war-related deaths have also increased (see Figure 1.3). 
Intrastate armed con icts are not only widespread, they also occur far 
more frequently than wars between states, even during times of increased 
international friction. In the post–World War II era, interstate war has been 
generally in decline, most notably in the period after the end of the Cold 
War. Although there has been an increase in international armed con ict 
since around 2010, the long-term historical trend is downward (Goldstein 
2011; Pinker 2011) – despite the perennial threat of such con ict and 
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In contrast, most 
wars have been within countries, and the armed con ict data indicate that 
there has been a steady increase in civil wars in recent decades. This rep 
resents a sharp resurgence in intrastate armed con ict in recent historical 
perspective, which has an enormous negative impact upon economic devel 
opment, human rights, forced human migration, and international order 
(United Nations and World Bank 2018) (Figure 1.2; see Appendix A). The 
direct human impacts of this violence and upheaval are concentrated in the 
Global South; according to the World Bank (2020), “By 2030, more than 
half of the world’s extreme poor will live in countries characterized by 
fragility, con ict, and violence.” But the broader consequences of civil war 
are global in nature in an interdependent world because these con icts are 
increasingly internationalized, and they form the battlegrounds of proxy 
con icts between powerful state actors.

3The Impacts of Civil War

In the period after the end of the Cold War, many analysts celebrated what they believed was a historical downturn in all forms of armed con ict, including civil war (Human Security Report Project 2005; Goldstein 2011;

Pinker 2011; Gat 2012). The reality, well into the twenty- rst century, is that civil wars and intrastate armed con ict are again at historic highs.

Understanding the direct and indirect causes, impacts, and dynamics of civil war is a compelling academic subject area, and it is also key to inform ing policies aimed at preventing civil war and building sustainable peace after widespread violence. This book provides a comprehensive primer on this evolving topic, presenting and engaging with the key theories, debates, cases, and controversies in the civil wars eld.

### The Impacts of Civil War

Civil wars have shaped and reshaped the modern world. They have a fun damental impact upon the political, economic, cultural, and social trajec tory of the societies involved, often leaving a very long legacy, including a recurrence of violence. These con icts are also closely linked to the changing international order, ecological degradation, identity, technologi cal changes, international intervention, and failures in global governance.

Civil wars – an increasing number of which are internationalized – are also linked to interstate con ict and to global geopolitical rivalries in a changing international order. They are rarely con ned to the territories in which they occur, since the consequences of civil wars – including

4 1 Introduction

forced migration, war economies, and insurgency – spill over borders. Most directly, civil wars have a cost measured in human lives. Data from the

Uppsala Con ict Data Program (UCDP) indicate that there were 1,928,205 battle-related deaths from intrastate and internationalized intrastate conicts worldwide from 1989 to 2023, compared to around 300,000 fatalities in interstate wars (UCDP 2024a) (Figure 1.3; see Appendix C). The indirect loss of life associated with civil wars – as a result of illness, deprivation, and the destruction of public services in con ict-affected societies – con tributes a far larger number of victims in the long term.

Adding to the direct and indirect loss of life are other tragic conse quences that affect the victims of these con icts. Gender-based violence, human rights abuses, the pernicious effects of war economies, mass atroc ities including war crimes and genocide, and environmental degradation are all consequences of intrastate armed con ict. As a part of this, a key international impact of civil wars – and a barometer of violence – is forced human displacement in the form of refugees and internally dis placed persons who have ed violence within their country’s borders (see

Chapter 3). According to the Of ce of the UN High Commissioner for

Refugees (UNHCR), 122.6 million people worldwide were forcibly dis placed in mid-2024 due to persecution, con ict, violence, human rights violations, or disorder. This represented an increase from 38 million in

2000 (UNHCR 2024).

5Themes of the Book

This increase in forced displacement is just one indication of the resur 
gence in civil war in recent years. Moreover, while forced human displace 
ment has been traditionally viewed as a secondary consequence of armed 
con ict, it is now readily apparent that refugees are often integral to the 
onset, dynamics, and nature of intrastate armed con ict, and a key com 
ponent of peacebuilding (the links between intrastate armed con ict and 
human displacement are explored in detail in Chapter 3). 
The broader scope and impact of civil wars are underpinned by the grow 
ing tendency in recent decades for them to be internationalized, re ecting 
increasing international military intervention and cross-border causes and 
effects (Figure 1.2; see Appendix A). This generally exacerbates the inten 
sity and length of violent con ict, and can draw in broader geopolitical 
rivalries, with a range of implications for international order and secu 
rity (Regan 2000; Bellamy 2023). Civil wars – such as those in Syria, the 
Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Afghanistan, Yemen, Sudan, and 
Iraq – have often been proxy con icts between powerful external states, at 
times raising the prospect of major international con ict. When civil wars 
involve separatist entities – such as the con ict in Ukraine since 2014 (see 
Box 12.2) and the earlier con ict in Kosovo – the risks of international 
escalation can be acute. The idea of civil wars as being discretely delineated 
by territorial borders has always been problematic for analytical purposes, 
and the links between civil wars and international peace and security have 
been amply demonstrated in the rst decades of the twenty- rst century. 

### Themes of the Book

This book explores a range of key questions and debates related to intra state armed con ict, in particular civil war: their driving forces and causes, nature and dynamics, how they are fought, the costs in life and livelihoods, their societal impact and international consequences, what explains their duration, how they end, and what makes them recur. Each chapter covers a key, substantive subject area related to civil wars and intrastate armed con ict in a self-contained manner, but there are also a number of overar ching themes to the book. First, a key feature of the book is its focus on con ict management and peacebuilding. Each chapter identi es links between its subject matter and con ict management and resolution (which encompasses mediation, con ict prevention, peace agreements, peacebuilding, and peacekeeping). This theme provides overarching coherence and puts the scholarly liter ature directly into conversation with the practitioner and policy-making

6 1 Introduction

community. Thus, an understanding of the causes and nature of civil war 
can inform con ict prevention strategies. Knowing the factors that affect 
con ict duration can strengthen policies aimed at bringing wars to an end 
and preventing recurrence. Knowledge of war recurrence and civil war– 
related terrorism can help shape better peace agreements and peacebuilding 
programs that are more likely to be resilient. Second, underlying con ict 
drivers – such as socioeconomic stresses, institutional fragilities, and envi 
ronmental degradation – form a key reference point throughout the book, 
in conjunction with other con ict dynamics and triggers. This means that 
the book brings together a signi cant amount of cross-national research 
ndings that have general explanatory relevance. Finally, the book seeks 
to be global in analytical orientation and grounded in empirical experience. 
It therefore places emphasis throughout upon case illustrations in order to 
explain how theoretical concepts in con ict analysis work in actual con- 
ict settings, both historically and in the contemporary world. 
The volume is designed to be theoretically rich while also being acces 
sible, covering a range of ongoing controversies in the eld. These 
include debates about the apparent increase in violence associated with 
religious identity, the question of whether major civil wars are declining 
or increasing in historical perspective, the relevance of climate change, 
and whether contemporary civil wars are qualitatively different in nature 
from those of the past. Thus, the book is distinctive in providing both a 
broad discussion of civil war topics – as a textbook – and also a discus 
sion of overarching debates about the causes, dynamics, and changing 
nature of civil war and intrastate armed con ict. As a teaching text, this 
book draws upon and synthesizes the existing secondary literature, but 
it also includes new insights drawn from various data sources, and in 
particular the UCDP.
